summary: Describes the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol, which keeps the caches of related servers in agreement. It is written mainly for non-broadcast multi-access networks, though it can be adapted for broadcast ones.

plainLanguage.summary: Several servers may each keep a record of the same clients. When one server's record changes, the others need to hear about it. This protocol covers the whole cycle: finding out who is connected, comparing what each server holds when they start up, and telling the others about changes afterwards.

subtitle: Keeps the caches of a group of servers in step, so each one knows the same thing about the clients it serves.

tldr.problem: When several servers hold the same information about clients, one server learning that the information has changed must tell the others, quickly and without overloading them.
tldr.mechanism: SCSP is a generic flooding protocol built on three sub-protocols: a Hello protocol that detects neighbours and the state of the link, a Cache Alignment protocol that compares summaries of cache entries at start-up, and a Cache State Update protocol that propagates changes afterwards. It borrows its cache distribution from the link state protocols.
tldr.outcome: Every server in the group ends up with the same view, and the system recovers from partitions and other failures because alignment runs whenever a link comes up. The document is not usable on its own: it needs a protocol-specific document that says what a cache entry means.

sections.title: The Problem and the Shape of the Solution
sections.content:
It is perhaps an obvious goal for any protocol not to limit itself to a single point of failure such as having a single server in a client/server paradigm. Even when there are redundant servers, the problem of cache synchronization remains: when one server becomes aware of a change in the state of cached information, that server must propagate the knowledge of the change to all servers which are actively mirroring that state information. This must be done in a timely fashion without putting undue strain on the servers.

Assuming that the state information kept in the server cache is the state of clients of the server, it is also highly desirable that clients need not have complete knowledge of all the servers which they may use. However, any mechanism for synchronization should not preclude a client from having access to several or all servers. Any solution must be reasonably scalable, capable of using some auto-configuration service, and lend itself to a wide range of authentication methodologies.

SCSP solves this generalized server synchronization and cache replication problem. It synchronizes the caches, or part of them, of a set of server entities of a particular protocol which are bound to a Server Group through some means, for example all NHRP servers belonging to a Logical IP Subnet. The client/server protocol is identified by a Protocol ID, and the server group by a Server Group ID, so the pair identifies both the protocol and the instance of that protocol, which means multiple instances of the same protocol can run at the same time and be synchronized independently.

The simplest way to understand SCSP is that the algorithm is quite similar to that used in OSPF. The protocol goes through three phases. The first, very brief phase is the hello phase where two devices determine that they can talk to each other. Following that is database synchronization, where the two neighbours exchange summary information about each entry in their database, since the database itself is potentially quite large, and request whatever each needs from the other. After that, the entities enter and remain in flooding state, where any new information that is learned is sent to all neighbours except the one it was learned from. Flooding is done reliably on each link.

The SCSP specification is not useful as a stand alone protocol. It must be coupled with an SCSP protocol-specific specification that defines how a given protocol makes use of the synchronization primitives.
sections.plainLanguage: The design follows the same shape as the routing protocol OSPF: shake hands, compare notes, then keep each other informed. On its own it knows nothing about what it is synchronizing, so another document has to say that.

sections.title: Terms and the Three Sub-Protocols
sections.content:
SCSP places no topological requirements upon the server group, but the resultant graph must span the set of servers to be synchronized. It borrows its cache distribution mechanism from the link state protocols, but unlike those technologies there is no mandatory Shortest Path First calculation, and SCSP imposes no additional memory requirements beyond that needed to save the cached information which would exist regardless of the synchronization technology.

Three terms give a frame of reference. The Local Server is the server under scrutiny, so all statements are made from its point of view. A Directly Connected Server is a server directly connected to the local server, for example with a virtual circuit between them; a Remote Server is a server that is not directly connected, and is therefore two or more hops away. Unless stated otherwise there is no implied difference in functionality between the three.

SCSP contains three sub-protocols. The Hello protocol ascertains whether a directly connected server is operational and whether the connection is bidirectional, unidirectional or non-functional. The Cache Alignment protocol allows a local server to synchronize its entire cache with the cache of each of its directly connected servers. The Cache State Update protocol is used to update the state of cache entries in servers for a given server group.

Synchronization is performed per protocol instance: a separate instance of SCSP is run for each instance of the given protocol running in a given box. The pair of protocol ID and server group ID uniquely identifies an instance. When many instances of a protocol run in the same box, a mechanism called the Family ID, described in the Hello protocol, enables a substantial reduction in maintenance traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server looks at the world from its own point of view: neighbours one hop away and everyone else further off. The work is split into three exchanges, and a server runs one copy of them per protocol it serves.

sections.title: The Hello Protocol
sections.content:
Hello messages ascertain whether a directly connected server is operational and whether the connections are bidirectional, unidirectional or non-functional. Every local server MUST periodically send a Hello message to its directly connected servers. The server is configured with a list of NBMA addresses representing the addresses of peer servers in the group to which it wishes to have a direct connection; the mechanism for that configuration is beyond the scope of the document, although one possible mechanism would be an autoconfiguration server.

Each local server has a Hello Finite State Machine for each of its directly connected servers, and that machine starts in the Down state and transitions to the Waiting state after NBMA level connectivity has been established. In the Waiting state the server starts sending Hello messages, each of which includes a Sender ID set to the server's own ID, zero or more Receiver IDs identifying the servers from which it has recently heard, and a HelloInterval and DeadFactor. When the local server receives a Hello from one of its neighbours it checks whether its own ID appears in one of the Receiver ID fields, and saves the Sender ID as the neighbour's ID. If its own ID is present the machine transitions to the Bidirectional Connection state, otherwise to the Unidirectional Connection state.

The HelloInterval advertises the time in seconds between consecutive Hello messages. If no Hello containing the local server's ID arrives within HelloInterval times DeadFactor seconds, where the DeadFactor was advertised by the neighbour in an earlier Hello, the neighbour MUST be considered stalled. At that point, if any Hello messages were received during that period the machine transitions to the Unidirectional Connection state; otherwise it transitions to the Waiting state and the neighbour's ID is removed from the Receiver ID list.

Hello messages contain a list of Receiver IDs instead of a single one so that point to multipoint connections can be used. While there is a state machine per neighbour, an local server MUST send only a single Hello message to the neighbours attached as leaves of a point to multipoint connection. Any abnormal event, such as receiving a malformed SCSP message, causes the machine to transition to the Waiting state, while a loss of NBMA connectivity causes it to transition to the Down state. Until the machine is in the Bidirectional Connection state, any properly formed SCSP messages other than Hello messages received MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side says hello on a timer and names the neighbours it has heard from. If the other side names you back, the link works both ways. If it stops naming you, the link is treated as stalled.

sections.title: The Cache Alignment Protocol
sections.content:
Cache Alignment messages are used by a local server to synchronize its cache with the cache of each of its directly connected servers, so that a booting server can synchronize with each of them. A CA message contains a CA header followed by zero or more Cache State Advertisement Summary records.

Each local server has a Cache Alignment Finite State Machine for each of its directly connected servers, on a per protocol and server group basis. It starts in the Down state and is associated with the Hello state machine: when that machine reaches the Bidirectional state, the alignment machine transitions to the Master/Slave Negotiation state, where either the local server or its neighbour takes on the role of master and sets the tempo for the alignment process.

The first CA message the local server sends contains no summary records and a header holding its own ID as Sender ID, the neighbour's ID as Receiver ID, a CA sequence number and three bits: the M bit for Master/Slave, the I bit for initialization of master, and the O bit for more. In that first message all three bits are set to one. If no CA message arrives from the neighbour within CAReXmtInterval seconds the message is resent, and this continues until the machine transitions to the Cache Summarize state or the Hello machine leaves the Bidirectional state. Whenever the Hello machine leaves the Bidirectional state, the alignment machine transitions to the Down state.

In the Master/Slave Negotiation state, if the CA from the neighbour has the M, I and O bits set, no summary records and a Sender ID larger than the local server's, the local server becomes the slave: it stops the retransmission timer, adopts the CA sequence number it received, and replies with the M and I bits clear and the same sequence number. If the CA from the neighbour has the M and I bits off and a Sender ID smaller than the local server's, the local server becomes the master: it stops the timer, processes the message, and replies with the M bit set, the I bit clear, and its CA sequence number incremented by one. Otherwise the packet is ignored.

In the Cache Summarize state, the master or the slave has at most one outstanding CA message. A message received with the M bit set incorrectly, or with the I bit set, sends the machine back to the Master/Slave Negotiation state. If the local server is master, a message whose sequence number is one less than its own is a duplicate and MUST be discarded, and a message whose sequence number equals its own must be processed, the summary records inside it handled, and the local sequence number incremented. If the local server is slave, a message whose sequence number equals its own is a duplicate and the local server resends the message it had just sent, while a message whose sequence number is one more is valid and must be processed. Any other sequence number is an error and sends the machine back to Master/Slave Negotiation.

Processing a CA message makes a list of the cache entries that are more up to date in the neighbour than in the local cache; this is the Cache State Advertisement Request List. In the Update Cache state, an empty list means the machine goes straight to the Aligned state. Otherwise the local server solicits the neighbour with Cache State Update Solicit messages built from the list, and the neighbour answers with one or more Cache State Update Request messages holding the full records. The local server may have at most one solicit outstanding at a time. A timer set to CSUSReXmtInterval seconds is started before the first solicit, and if the records have not all arrived when it expires, a new solicit is created with the records still missing plus additional ones, and the process continues until the cache is completely updated and the machine reaches the Aligned state.
sections.plainLanguage: When two servers start up, one of them takes the lead and they exchange short summaries of what they hold. Where the neighbour has something newer, the first asks for the full record, and only then are they in step.

sections.title: The Cache State Update Protocol
sections.content:
Cache State Update messages are used to update the state of cache entries in servers for a given protocol and server group. A CSU message contains zero or more Cache State Advertisement records, each of which holds its own snapshot of the state of a particular cache entry. A local server may send or receive a CSU only when the corresponding alignment machine is in the Aligned state or the Update Cache state.

There are two types of CSU message, requests and replies. A CSU Request is sent to one or more directly connected servers for one of two reasons: the local server has received a solicit and must respond only to the server that sent it, or the local server has become aware of a change of state of a cache entry. A change is noticed either by receiving a CSU Request from a neighbour or by observing a change in a cached entry the local server originated. In the first case the local server sends a CSU Request to each of its neighbours except the one it heard from; in the second it sends one to each of them. The change is noted in a Cache State Advertisement record appended to the mandatory part of the CSU Request, and in this way state changes are propagated throughout the group.

Examples of such changes are a server receiving a request from a client to add an entry to its cache, a request to remove an entry, and a cache entry timing out, being refreshed, or being administratively modified.

When a local server receives a CSU Request it acknowledges the records it accepted by sending a CSU Reply holding the corresponding summary records. If a record was dropped or delayed for lack of resources, no matching summary record is included. The terms request and reply are a bit confusing: a local server may send several CSU Requests before receiving any reply, and a reply may acknowledge records from several requests.

For each neighbour a timer set to CSUReXmtInterval seconds is started just before a CSU Request is sent, and if the timer expires before all the records have been acknowledged a new request is sent containing only the records not yet acknowledged. Retransmission occurs a configured number of times, and if acknowledgment then fails an abnormal event has occurred and the Hello state machine for that neighbour transitions to the Waiting state. Only the most up to date record is permitted to be queued to a given neighbour, so a newer record deplaces an older one.

A record is acknowledged when an exact match is found in a reply, and the matching queued record is removed. If the match differs only in the sequence number, a reply with a larger sequence number means the queued record is removed and a solicit is sent to that server for the newer record, while a reply with a smaller sequence number is ignored. If a CSU Request carries a record whose sequence number is smaller than the one cached, the record is acknowledged but with the cached summary rather than the one in the request. A solicit for an entry that no longer exists in the cache is answered with a record marked as a NULL record by setting the N bit. A CSU with a Receiver ID that is neither the local server's ID nor the all 0xFFs value must be discarded, since the server may be a leaf of a point to multipoint connection with other servers in the group.
sections.plainLanguage: After start-up, a server that learns something new sends it to all its neighbours except the one it heard it from, and keeps resending it until the neighbours confirm. If an entry has expired, it sends a record that says so.

sections.title: Deciding Which Record Is Newer
sections.content:
During cache alignment and during normal processing, a summary record is compared against the contents of a local server's cache entry to decide whether the record is more up to date than the cached entry.

Three pieces of information are used: the Cache Key, the Originator, described by an Originator ID, and the CSA Sequence number. A summary record, whether it is part of a full record or stands alone, is considered more up to date than the information in the cache of a local server if all of the following are true: the Cache Key in the record matches the stored Cache Key in the local cache entry, the Originator ID in the record matches the stored Originator ID, and the CSA Sequence Number in the record is greater than the CSA Sequence Number in the local cache entry.
sections.plainLanguage: A record replaces a cached one only when it refers to the same entry, comes from the same original source, and carries a higher number.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
SCSP protocols are LLC/SNAP encapsulated with an LLC value of 0xAA-AA-03, an OUI of 0x00-00-5e and a PID of 0x00-05. Every packet has three parts: the fixed part, the mandatory part and the extensions part. Fields marked as unused MUST be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The fixed part is present in every packet and holds a Version field, whose current value is 1, a Type Code for the message type, a Packet Size giving the total length of the SCSP packet in octets excluding link layer and other encapsulation, a Checksum which is the standard IP checksum over the entire SCSP packet starting at the fixed header, and a Start Of Extensions field which is coded zero when no extensions are present and otherwise holds the offset from the top of the fixed header to the first extension.

The mandatory part is specific to the message type and includes a Mandatory Common Part plus zero or more records. The common part holds the Protocol ID, the Server Group ID, an unused field, the Flags field, a Sender ID Length, a Receiver ID Length, a Number of Records, the Sender ID and the Receiver ID, both of variable length. The type codes are CA 1, CSU Request 2, CSU Reply 3, CSUS 4 and Hello 5. Protocol IDs with current documents are 1 for ATMARP, 2 for NHRP, 3 for MARS, 4 for DHCP and 5 for LNNI.

The Cache State Advertisement Summary record holds a Hop Count, a Record Length, a Cache Key Length, an Originator ID Length, an N bit, the CSA Sequence Number, the Cache Key and the Originator ID. The Hop Count is the number of hops the record may take before being dropped, decremented at each server; it is set to 1 for a stand-alone record, since summaries do not go beyond one hop during alignment, and to an administratively defined value when the record is embedded, almost certainly greater than or equal to the size of the group minus one. The N bit marks a record as a NULL record. The CSA Sequence Number is a signed 32-bit number; the value -2^31 is reserved, so the usable range for a given cache key runs from -2^31+1 to 2^31-1. A local server uses -2^31+1 the first time it originates a record for a cache entry it created, and increments the number each time the entry is modified and the change must be synchronized. If the number reaches 2^31-2 and the entry must be updated again, the entry is first purged from the group with a record carrying 2^31-1, and after that purge is acknowledged a new record with -2^31+1 is sent.

The extensions part, when present, carries one or more extensions in Type, Length and Value triplets. It is terminated by the End of Extensions extension with Type 0 and Length 0, and any particular extension type may occur only once in a packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has the same three-part layout: a small fixed header, a part that depends on the message type, and optional extra fields at the end.

sections.title: Authentication and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The SCSP Authentication Extension is carried in SCSP packets to convey authentication information between a local server and a directly connected server in the same group. Authentication is done pairwise, so the extension is generated at each local server. If a received packet fails the authentication test an abnormal event has occurred: the packet is discarded and the event is logged. The presence or absence of authentication is a local matter.

The authentication header holds a Security Parameter Index and the authentication data. The index can be thought of as an index into a table that holds the keys and other information such as the hash algorithm; the local server and its neighbour communicate either off-line using manual keying or online using a key management protocol to populate the table, and the receiving entity always allocates the index and its parameters. The authentication data holds the Message Authentication Code calculated over the entire SCSP payload, and its length depends on the hash algorithm used. The default hash algorithm to be supported is HMAC-MD5-128. SPIs can be negotiated either manually or using an Internet key management protocol, and manual keying must be supported; the parameters associated with the tuple of index and neighbour ID are the lifetime in seconds, the algorithm and the key.

On the security considerations themselves: the keys chosen must be strong, since the security of the entire system depends on the keys being chosen properly and the algorithms being implemented correctly. SCSP has a peer to peer trust model, so an Internet standard key management protocol is recommended, and transmitting the keys in clear text compromises the security completely. Data integrity covers the entire SCSP payload, which guarantees the message was not modified and the source is authenticated; if the authentication extension is not used, or the security is compromised, SCSP servers are liable to spoofing, active and passive attacks. There is no mechanism to encrypt the messages, and a standard layer 3 confidentiality mechanism is assumed. Because integrity is calculated on a whole message and not on each record, there is an implied trust between all the servers in a domain, and it is recommended to use the security extension between all the servers in a domain and not just a subset. Any SCSP server is susceptible to denial of service attacks, but if the authentication option is used the databases will not become corrupted, because the bogus packets are discarded when the check fails. Because of the pairwise authentication model, information received from any properly authenticated server is trusted and propagated throughout the server group, so if the security of any server is compromised the entire database becomes vulnerable to corruption originating from it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each neighbour pair can protect its messages with a keyed code, and packets that fail the check are thrown away. The messages are not encrypted, and a server that is compromised can pass on bad data to the whole group.
